10.8. Certified Integration🔗

10.8.1. Certified Quadrature🔗

A quadrature certificate bounds the difference between a proposed value and the integral. Exactness on polynomials and bounds on derivatives control the analytic error; interval evaluation controls the error in computing the finite weighted sum. These two errors add.

A quadrature certificate stores a proposed value of a Bochner interval integral, an explicit error budget, and a proof of the corresponding norm estimate. The certificate is indexed by the ordinary Lean integrand and endpoints, so no symbolic expression type appears in theorem statements.

Its trusted field is

q.\mathrm{sound}:\qquad \left\|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx-q.\mathrm{value}\right\| \leq q.\mathrm{error}.

A complete certificate: Simpson on x^2.

Take f(x)=x^2 on [0,1]. One Simpson panel uses the values at 0, 1/2, and 1, so its exact-real value is

\frac16 f(0)+\frac46 f\left(\frac12\right)+\frac16 f(1) =\frac13.

Because Simpson's rule is exact for every polynomial of degree at most three, its quadrature certificate has:

  • the stored value is 1/3;

  • the stored error is 0;

  • soundness proves \left|\int_0^1x^2\,dx-\frac13\right|\leq0.

The third field is the mathematical content. The first two fields are data that later planners can inspect and combine. Since the integrand is a continuous polynomial, it is also interval integrable; that fact is separate because QuadratureCert itself is stated for Mathlib's totalized interval integral.

For a nonpolynomial integrand, the shape of the object is unchanged. A Simpson or Gauss–Legendre theorem supplies a positive analytic error, and a verified numerical backend may replace the exact-real weighted sum with a computed value by adding a separately proved roundoff error. The final sound field always states one inequality about the original integral.

The first polynomial beyond Simpson's exactness range shows what the error constant measures. For f(x)=x^4 on [0,1],

S(f)=\frac46\frac1{16}+\frac16=\frac5{24}, \qquad \int_0^1x^4\,dx=\frac15, \qquad S(f)-\int_0^1f=\frac1{120}.

Here f^{(4)}=24, so the sharp Simpson bound is 24/2880=1/120, exactly the observed error. The fourth derivative measures the first behavior that the degree-three exactness does not reproduce.

A final triangle inequality adds this model error to the existing quadrature error.

If the scalar integrand is interval integrable and one backend interval contains every value on [[a,b]], its midpoint defines a constant integral model and its radius gives the uniform pointwise error. The resulting certificate has value (b-a)c and error r|b-a|, with no endpoint-order assumption and no backend-specific integration theorem. Exact rational ranges, directed floating-point ranges, Taylor enclosures, and adaptive local ranges therefore share the same analytic bridge.

Proof for Theorem 10.85
uses 0

Write the enclosure as center c and radius r. Interval membership gives |f(x)-c|\leq r uniformly, so integration stability compares f with the constant function c. The constant integral is (b-a)c, and its transported error is r|b-a|.

How the error budget is assembled.

A certificate constructor assembles the error budget in five steps:

  1. prove exactness on a polynomial model or prove a Peano-kernel remainder;

  2. obtain any required derivative bound as an ordinary theorem;

  3. sum local analytic errors when the interval is subdivided;

  4. enclose the finite weighted sum if it is evaluated numerically;

  5. add the proved roundoff radius to the analytic budget.

The quadrature rule chooses nodes and weights. The derivative theorem controls truncation. The numerical backend controls finite evaluation. Keeping those proofs separate makes it possible to replace one backend or one subdivision policy without changing the statement about the integral.

Quadrature rules implemented.

The certificate constructors use four normalized rules, each stored as an exact list of (weight, node) pairs on [0,1]. Each error formula assumes the stated derivative bound and the corresponding C^2 or C^4 regularity on an ordered interval [a,b].

  • Trapezoidal rule: two nodes at \{0, 1\} with weights \{1/2, 1/2\}. Exact for polynomials of degree at most 1. Error on [a,b]: \zeta(b-a)^3/12 where \zeta bounds |f''|.

  • Midpoint rule: one node at 1/2 with weight 1. Exact for polynomials of degree at most 1. Error on [a,b]: \zeta(b-a)^3/24, half the trapezoid constant.

  • Simpson's rule: three nodes at \{0, 1/2, 1\} with weights \{1/6, 4/6, 1/6\}. Exact for polynomials of degree at most 3. The sharp Peano-kernel error on [a,b]: C(b-a)^5/2880 where C bounds |f^{(4)}|.

  • Two-point Gauss–Legendre: two nodes at \{1/2 - 1/(2\sqrt{3}), 1/2 + 1/(2\sqrt{3})\} with weights \{1/2, 1/2\}. With only two nodes it is exact for polynomials of degree at most 3, like Simpson's three-node rule. The sharp Peano-kernel error: C(b-a)^5/4320, which is 2/3 of Simpson's error constant.

The Gauss–Legendre rule has irrational nodes (1/2 \pm \sqrt{3}/6), which are represented exactly in the real-valued QuadratureRule. Numerical evaluation encloses the exact weighted terms by proved intervals. A RationalQuadratureRule, by contrast, has rational nodes.

The Peano kernel approach.

The sharp error constants (1/2880 for Simpson, 1/4320 for Gauss–Legendre) come from the Peano kernel method. For a rule Q that is exact on polynomials of degree at most d and an integrand f \in C^{d+1}[a,b], the integration error equals

\int_a^b f(x)\,dx - Q(f) = \int_a^b K_{d+1}(t) f^{(d+1)}(t)\,dt,

where K_{d+1} is the Peano kernel of order d+1: the functional f \mapsto \int f - Q(f) applied to the truncated power (x-t)_+^d / d!. If K_{d+1} has constant sign, the integral is bounded by \|f^{(d+1)}\|_\infty \cdot \int |K_{d+1}|.

Example: composite Simpson on \int_0^1 e^x\,dx.

First plan the exact-real composite value to analytic tolerance \tau = 10^{-8}. A computed replacement must also fit its evaluation error within the remaining budget before claiming this same total tolerance.

  1. Derivative bound. On [0,1], f^{(4)}(x) = e^x \leq e < 3. Set C = 3.

  2. Error constant. B = C(b-a)^5/2880 = 3/2880 = 1/960.

  3. Panel planning. Solve B/N^4 \leq \tau: N \geq (B/\tau)^{1/4} = (10^8/960)^{1/4} \approx 17.97. The planner rounds up to N = 18: exactly, 960\cdot17^4<10^8\leq960\cdot18^4.

  4. Certificate construction. Build 18 Simpson panels of width 1/18. Summing their sharp errors gives 1/(960\cdot18^4)\approx9.923\times10^{-9}<10^{-8}.

  5. Value computation. The panel-major schedule contains 54 weighted samples, with 2\cdot18+1=37 distinct nodes because adjacent endpoints coincide. A numerical backend must provide enclosures for those samples and their weighted sum; the analytic panel count alone supplies no evaluation precision.

  6. Final certificate. The QuadratureCert stores:

    • value: the midpoint of the weighted-sum enclosure,

    • error: the analytic Simpson error plus the weighted-sum roundoff radius,

    • sound: the proof that |\int_0^1 e^x\,dx - \text{value}| \leq \text{error}.

This final error is at most 10^{-8} only if the certified evaluation radius is at most 10^{-8}-1/(960\cdot18^4). Otherwise, refine the evaluation or replan the analytic mesh with a smaller reserved budget.

Adaptive quadrature and the tree structure.

Composite rules use a fixed number of equal panels, which may be inefficient for integrands with localized difficulty (near-singularities, rapid oscillation). The adaptive framework addresses this with a binary QuadratureTree whose leaves are local certificates and whose branches split an interval at a point. Because soundness depends only on the leaf certificates and their composition, an adaptive algorithm may choose the subdivision by any heuristic, including Richardson extrapolation, derivative estimates, or a priori knowledge of integrand behavior.

A normalized quadrature rule is an ordered list of exact-real weights and nodes in [0,1]. The order remains explicit for verified finite-precision evaluation. Generic definitions transport the rule affinely to any oriented interval, while moment identities characterize exactness independently of a particular numerical backend.

used by 1✓L∃∀N

The rational algebraic fragment of the shared expression language has a fail-closed exact evaluator. Every successful result is proved equal to the existing real expression semantics. A quadrature rule with rational weights and nodes can therefore sample a symbolic integrand exactly, preserve the ordered rule schedule, and cast term-for-term to the existing transported QuadratureRule. Transcendental nodes, malformed literals, and sampled zero denominators are rejected. Optional finite-precision backends consume the exact table through the same interval and weighted-sum interfaces.

At the expression boundary,

\operatorname{evalRat?}(e,\rho)=\operatorname{some}(q) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{eval}(e,\rho_{\mathbb R})=(q:\mathbb R).

For a successfully compiled rule, casting every rational term preserves the analytic schedule and value:

\operatorname{cast}\!\left(\sum_j w_j e(x_j)\right) =\sum_j (w_j:\mathbb R)\, \operatorname{eval}(e,(x_j:\mathbb R)).

Proof for Theorem 10.87
uses 0

Prove the rational evaluator correct by structural induction on the algebraic expression, rejecting precisely the division cases with zero denominator. Apply that equality at each rational quadrature node. Casting commutes with the finite products and sum, so the compiled ordered table has the same real weighted value as the analytic rule.

If a normalized rule has the exact moments through degree d, it exactly integrates every real polynomial of degree at most d. Affine transport preserves this conclusion on arbitrary oriented intervals. Both the three-node Simpson rule and the two-point Gauss–Legendre rule have the exact moments through degree three, hence exactly integrate every cubic and generate zero-error QuadratureCerts.

If two scalar integrands differ uniformly by \varepsilon on [[a,b]], their values under a normalized rule differ by at most |b-a|\,V\varepsilon, where V is the sum of the absolute rule weights. This estimate lets a rule that is exact on a nearby model be evaluated on the original integrand while accounting separately for integral-model error and sample-value perturbation.

    The first error term controls the difference of the two interval integrals. The second controls the difference between rule evaluations at their sampled nodes. A backend may then replace this exact-real sampled value with the midpoint of an enclosing interval through QuadratureCert.replaceValue (or QuadratureCert.replaceValueOfInterval in Core).

Proof for Theorem 10.89
uses 0

At every node, the sample difference is at most \varepsilon. Apply the triangle inequality to the weighted sum, bound each term by |w_j|\varepsilon, and sum to obtain V\varepsilon on the normalized interval. Affine transport contributes the factor |b-a|.

10.8.1.1. Nodes, weights, and degree of exactness🔗

A normalized rule lives on [0,1] and is moved to [a,b] affinely. For the general theory it is simpler to let the nodes sit anywhere on the real line and to integrate against a weight function. A NodalRule is just that: m real nodes x_i and m real weights w_i, with value Q(f)=\sum_i w_i f(x_i). It carries no interval and no weight function of its own. Exactness is a property relative to an interval and a weight, which is what lets one rule be read against several weights, and it is stated with Mathlib's interval integral, so exactness does not assert integrability.

The central number attached to a rule is its degree of exactness, the largest d such that Q(p)=\int_a^b p\,w for every polynomial of degree at most d. The trapezoid and midpoint rules have degree one, Simpson's rule three, and a Gauss rule with n nodes 2n-1. A high degree of exactness is what turns smoothness of f into a small error: if f is close to some polynomial of degree d, a rule exact to degree d can only see the difference.

A nodal rule consists of a size m, nodes x_0,\dots,x_{m-1}\in\mathbb R, and weights w_0,\dots,w_{m-1}\in\mathbb R. It is exact to degree d for the weight w on a..b when

\sum_{i<m} w_i\,p(x_i)=\int_a^b p(x)\,w(x)\,dx \qquad\text{for every real polynomial }p\text{ with }\deg p\le d.

It is positive when every w_i\ge0, and its nodes lie in s when every x_i\in s. A normalized QuadratureRule becomes a nodal rule on [a,b] with nodes a+t_i(b-a) and weights (b-a)w_i.

used by 1✓L∃∀N

For a weight continuous on [[a,b]], a nodal rule is exact to degree d exactly when it integrates the monomials 1,x,\dots,x^d. Exactness moves with the rule under the affine map sending a,b to c,d: if Q is exact to degree n on [a,b] for the pulled-back weight, the transported rule, with nodes mapped and weights scaled by (d-c)/(b-a), is exact to degree n on [c,d] for the original weight. A normalized rule with the moments through degree d is exact to degree d on every interval for the unit weight, and a normalized rule with nonnegative weights is positive on every ordered interval.

Proof for Theorem 10.91
uses 0

Both sides of the exactness identity are linear in the integrand, so a polynomial written in the monomial basis reduces to its monomials. The continuity of w supplies the integrability that splitting the integral needs. For transport, substitute x=c+(t-a)(d-c)/(b-a): the change of variables formula turns \int_c^d f\,v into (d-c)/(b-a) times an integral over [a,b], and composing a polynomial with an affine map does not raise its degree.

The most direct way to obtain exactness is to integrate an interpolant. Given m distinct nodes, let \ell_i be the Lagrange basis polynomial that is 1 at x_i and 0 at the other nodes, and put w_i=\int_a^b\ell_i\,w. A polynomial p of degree below m equals its interpolant \sum_i p(x_i)\ell_i, so integrating gives Q(p)=\int_a^b p\,w. With equally spaced nodes including both endpoints this is the closed Newton–Cotes family: two points give the trapezoid rule and three give Simpson's rule.

Let w be continuous on [[a,b]] and let x_0,\dots,x_{m-1} be m\ge1 distinct nodes. The interpolatory rule with weights w_i=\int_a^b\ell_i\,w is exact to degree m-1. For n\ge2 and a\ne b, the closed Newton–Cotes rule on the nodes a+i(b-a)/(n-1), i=0,\dots,n-1, is exact to degree n-1 for the unit weight; its nodes lie in [a,b] when a\le b, and for n=2 its value is \frac{b-a}2\bigl(f(a)+f(b)\bigr).

Proof for Theorem 10.92
uses 0

A polynomial of degree below m coincides with its Lagrange interpolant on the m nodes, and the rule applied to it is the integral of that interpolant against w. The Newton–Cotes nodes are distinct because the spacing (b-a)/(n-1) is nonzero. For two nodes the Lagrange basis polynomials are linear and each integrates to (b-a)/2.

Interpolation fixes m weights from m nodes, and the resulting degree m-1 is all that can be said for a general choice of nodes. Simpson's rule does better than its three nodes promise, reaching degree three, because its middle node sits at the symmetric point. Gaussian quadrature asks how far this can go when all the nodes are free.

10.8.1.2. Orthogonal polynomials🔗

Fix a weight w that is continuous and strictly positive on [a,b], a<b. The pairing

\langle p,q\rangle=\int_a^b p(x)\,q(x)\,w(x)\,dx

is an inner product on real polynomials: it is bilinear and symmetric, and \langle p,p\rangle>0 for p\ne0, because a nonzero polynomial has only finitely many zeros, so p^2w is positive on some open subinterval. Orthogonalizing 1,x,x^2,\dots gives one monic polynomial p_n of each degree, orthogonal to every polynomial of lower degree. For the unit weight on [-1,1] these are the monic Legendre polynomials

p_1=x,\qquad p_2=x^2-\tfrac13,\qquad p_3=x^3-\tfrac35x,\qquad p_4=x^4-\tfrac67x^2+\tfrac3{35}.

More generally, a linear functional L on \mathbb R[X] that is positive on nonzero squares defines the inner product \langle p,q\rangle=L(pq). Subtracting the orthogonal projection of X^n onto polynomials of degree below n constructs p_n. Integration against a positive weight is one instance.

Let L:\mathbb R[X]\to\mathbb R be linear with L(q^2)>0 for every q\ne0. The monic orthogonal polynomial p_n of L is monic of degree n and satisfies L(p_nq)=0 for every q with \deg q<n. It is unique: any monic polynomial of degree n with this property equals p_n. For a weight w continuous on [[a,b]] and strictly positive on [a,b], a<b, the functional p\mapsto\int_a^b p\,w is positive on nonzero squares, and its orthogonal polynomials are the ones used for Gaussian quadrature.

Uniqueness is short and gets used repeatedly. If p and p_n are both monic of degree n and orthogonal to lower degrees, their difference r has degree below n, so L(r^2)=L(pr)-L(p_nr)=0, and positivity forces r=0. Every identification of a concrete polynomial with p_n goes through this argument.

Orthogonal polynomials satisfy a three-term recurrence. Since xp_{n+1} is monic of degree n+2, the difference xp_{n+1}-p_{n+2} has degree at most n+1, and its expansion in p_0,\dots,p_{n+1} has only two nonzero coefficients: for k<n the coefficient of p_k is proportional to L(xp_{n+1}p_k)=L(p_{n+1}\cdot xp_k), which vanishes because xp_k has degree below n+1.

Proof for Theorem 10.94
uses 0

The right side is monic of degree n+2. It is orthogonal to p_{n+1} by the choice of \alpha_{n+1}, to p_n by the choice of \beta_n, and to every polynomial of degree below n because L(xp_{n+1}p_k)=0 for k<n. Uniqueness identifies it with p_{n+2}. For the second formula, xp_n-p_{n+1} has degree at most n, so orthogonality of p_{n+1} gives L(xp_{n+1}p_n)=L(p_{n+1}^2).

For the unit weight on [-1,1] the symmetry x\mapsto-x makes every \alpha_n vanish. From L(1)=2 and L(p_1^2)=\tfrac23 one gets \beta_0=\tfrac13 and p_2=x^2-\tfrac13; then L(p_2^2)=\tfrac8{45}, \beta_1=\tfrac4{15}, and p_3=x\,p_2-\tfrac4{15}x=x^3-\tfrac35x, as in the Legendre list.

The roots of p_n are the nodes of the Gauss rule, and three facts about them are needed: they are real, simple, and inside (a,b). All three come from one observation. Suppose q divides p_n, say p_n=qr with \deg r<n. Orthogonality gives \int_a^b q\,r^2w=\int_a^b p_n\,r\,w=0. If q had no zero on [a,b] it would have constant sign there, and so would qr^2w, which is not identically zero; the integral could not vanish. So every nonconstant factor of p_n has a root in [a,b].

Let w be continuous on [[a,b]] and strictly positive on [a,b], a<b, and let p\ne0 be orthogonal against w to every polynomial of lower degree. Then every nonconstant divisor of p has a root in [a,b], p is squarefree and splits over \mathbb R, and every root of p lies in the open interval (a,b). Consequently the monic orthogonal polynomial p_n has exactly n distinct real roots, all in (a,b), and they can be listed as x_0,\dots,x_{n-1} so that the nodal polynomial \prod_i(x-x_i) equals p_n.

Proof for Theorem 10.95
uses 0

The divisor statement is the sign argument for \int_a^b q\,r^2w. An irreducible real factor of degree two has no real root, so it cannot divide p, and p splits. If q^2 divides p with q nonconstant, write p=q^2r; then L((qr)^2)=L(p\,r)=0, contradicting positivity, so p is squarefree. A root at the endpoint a would give p=(x-a)r with \int_a^b(x-a)\,r^2w=0, but (x-a)w is a weight that is positive on the interior; the endpoint b is symmetric. A monic squarefree polynomial that splits is the product of x-x_i over its distinct roots.

The figure lists the roots of p_n for the Legendre weight, n=1 to 8, and draws P_n, the Legendre polynomial rescaled so that P_n(1)=1, for the highlighted row. The roots stay strictly inside (-1,1), as the theorem requires, and they crowd toward the endpoints as n grows. The disc areas are the Gauss weights constructed next.

10.8.1.3. Gaussian quadrature🔗

The degree of exactness of a rule with n nodes can never reach 2n. The nodal polynomial \omega(x)=\prod_i(x-x_i) has degree n, so \omega^2 has degree 2n; the rule returns \sum_iw_i\omega(x_i)^2=0, while \int_a^b\omega^2w>0. Gauss's theorem says that degree 2n-1 is reached, for one choice of nodes only.

Why must the nodes be the roots of p_n? Suppose a rule with nodes x_i is exact to degree 2n-1. For any q of degree below n the product \omega q has degree below 2n, and it vanishes at every node, so

\int_a^b\omega\,q\,w=Q(\omega q)=\sum_i w_i\,\omega(x_i)\,q(x_i)=0.

Thus \omega is monic of degree n and orthogonal to all lower degrees, and uniqueness forces \omega=p_n. Conversely, take the nodes to be the roots of p_n and the weights interpolatory. Any p of degree below 2n divides as p=p_nq+r with \deg q,\deg r<n. The rule sees only r, since p_n vanishes at the nodes, and it integrates r exactly; the integral sees only r as well, since \int p_nq\,w=0. So Q(p)=\int_a^b p\,w.

Let w be continuous on [[a,b]] and strictly positive on [a,b], a<b, and let n\ge1. There are n distinct nodes in (a,b) whose interpolatory weights w_i=\int_a^b\ell_i\,w are all strictly positive and for which

\sum_{i<n}w_i\,p(x_i)=\int_a^b p(x)\,w(x)\,dx\qquad\text{whenever }\deg p<2n.

As a NodalRule, the rule is positive, has its nodes in [a,b], and is exact to degree 2n-1.

Proof for Theorem 10.96
uses 0

Take the nodes to be the roots of p_n. The interpolatory rule on n distinct nodes reproduces every polynomial of degree below n. For \deg p<2n, divide by the monic nodal polynomial: the quotient term is annihilated by the rule, because the nodal polynomial vanishes at the nodes, and by the integral, by orthogonality; the remainder has degree below n. For the weights, apply exactness to \ell_i^2, which has degree 2n-2: the rule returns w_i, and the integral \int_a^b\ell_i^2w is positive.

The nodes determine the weights, and the weights are positive. This positivity will give convergence for continuous integrands.

uses 1used by 1✓L∃∀N

A Gaussian rule with n nodes for the weight w on [a,b] is a structure GaussianRule a b w hw n, where hw records that w is continuous on [[a,b]]. It holds nodes x_0,\dots,x_{n-1}, weights w_0,\dots,w_{n-1}, and four facts: the nodes are pairwise distinct, they lie in the open interval (a,b), the weights are strictly positive, and

\sum_{i<n}w_i\,p(x_i)=\int_a^b p(x)\,w(x)\,dx\qquad\text{whenever }\deg p<2n.

Its value on a function f is \sum_iw_if(x_i). For n=0 the rule is empty and the exactness field says nothing, so the theorems about Gaussian rules assume n>0.

    positive : ∀ (i : Fin n), 0 < self.weights i

For a<b, a weight that is strictly positive on [a,b], and n>0, gaussianRule is the Gaussian rule of the existence theorem, with nodes at the roots of p_n and interpolatory weights. Every Gaussian rule with n>0 is a positive NodalRule exact to degree 2n-1. Exactness on the constant 1 makes its weights add up to \int_a^b w, so each weight is at most \int_a^b w.

For every Gaussian rule with n nodes for a continuous weight that is strictly positive on [a,b], the nodal polynomial \prod_i(x-x_i) is the monic orthogonal polynomial p_n of w, and the weight at x_i is the interpolatory weight \int_a^b\ell_i\,w, the Christoffel number. A Gaussian rule is therefore unique up to the order of its nodes.

Proof for Theorem 10.99
uses 0

The nodal polynomial times any q of degree below n has degree below 2n and vanishes at every node, so its integral is its rule value, zero. Uniqueness of the monic orthogonal polynomial identifies the nodal polynomial. For the weights, apply exactness to \ell_i, which has degree n-1 and takes the value 1 at x_i and 0 at the other nodes.

The figure shows both halves of the argument for n=3 and the Legendre weight. On the left, p_3(x)\,x has degree four; the rule returns zero, and orthogonality makes the integral zero too. On the right, p_3^2 has degree six; the rule still returns zero, but the integral is \tfrac8{175}. That positive number reappears as the constant in the error formula.

The error of a Gauss rule is found by comparing f with its Hermite interpolant H, the polynomial of degree below 2n that matches f and f' at the n nodes. The rule is exact on H and cannot tell f from H, so the error is \int_a^b(f-H)\,w. The pointwise remainder is the familiar one for interpolation, with every node counted twice:

f(x)-H(x)=\frac{f^{(2n)}(\eta_x)}{(2n)!}\,\omega(x)^2 \qquad\text{for some }\eta_x\in[a,b].

Because \omega^2w\ge0, a mean-value argument for the integral pulls the derivative out at a single point.

uses 1used by 0✓L∃∀N

Let w be continuous on [[a,b]] and strictly positive on [a,b], a<b, let Q be a Gaussian rule with n\ge1 nodes, and let f\in C^{2n} on [a,b]. There is \xi\in[a,b] with

\int_a^b f(x)\,w(x)\,dx-Q(f) =\frac{f^{(2n)}(\xi)}{(2n)!}\int_a^b \omega(x)^2\,w(x)\,dx,

where \omega=\prod_i(x-x_i) is the nodal polynomial, equal to p_n by the characterization. Here f^{(2n)} is the iterated derivative within [a,b], so smoothness is needed only on the closed interval. If |f^{(2n)}|\le M on [a,b], the error is at most M/(2n)!\,\int_a^bp_n^2w.

    Pointwise Hermite remainder for a derivative chain F on [a, b] and n distinct nodes there. At every x ∈ [a, b] some ξ ∈ [a, b] satisfies F 0 x - H x = F (2n) ξ / (2n)! * P x ^ 2, with H the Hermite interpolant of F 0, F 1 at the nodes and P the nodal polynomial. At a node both sides vanish. Otherwise G = F 0 - H - c P ^ 2 with c = (F 0 x - H x) / P x ^ 2 has double zeros at the nodes and a zero at x, so exists_derivative_chain_zero_of_double_zeros gives ξ with G^(2n) ξ = 0, and H^(2n) = 0, (P ^ 2)^(2n) = (2n)! unwind this to the claim.

Proof for Theorem 10.100
uses 0

Fix x away from the nodes and choose c so that G=f-H-c\,\omega^2 vanishes at x. Then G has double zeros at the n nodes and a simple zero at x, 2n+1 zeros counted with multiplicity. A generalized Rolle theorem, proved for a chain of functions each the derivative of the previous one on the open interval, gives a zero \eta_x of G^{(2n)}. Since H^{(2n)}=0 and (\omega^2)^{(2n)}=(2n)!, this is the pointwise remainder. Multiply by w and integrate. The continuous function f^{(2n)} takes values between its minimum and maximum on [a,b], so the integral of (f-H)w lies between those extremes times \int\omega^2w, and the intermediate value theorem produces \xi. Finally \omega=p_n by the characterization.

For n=2 and the Legendre weight the constant is \int_{-1}^1p_2^2=\tfrac8{45}. Rescaled to an interval of length h, where \int p_2^2 scales by (h/2)^5, the formula gives error f^{(4)}(\xi)\,h^5/4320, the same constant as the sharp two-point Gauss–Legendre certificate, which is proved by a Peano kernel. For n=3 the constant on [-1,1] is \tfrac8{175}/6!=\tfrac1{15750}.

The first four Gauss–Legendre rules have closed forms in radicals. On [-1,1] the one-point rule is the midpoint rule with weight 2, the two-point rule has nodes \pm1/\sqrt3 and weights 1, the three-point rule has nodes 0,\pm\sqrt{3/5} and weights \tfrac89,\tfrac59, and the four-point rule has nodes \pm\sqrt{(15\mp2\sqrt{30})/35} with weights (18\pm\sqrt{30})/36, the larger weight at the inner pair. The library stores them in the normalized convention on [0,1], checks the moments degree by degree, and then identifies each with the orthogonal-polynomial construction.

used by 0✓L∃∀N

The normalized three- and four-point Gauss–Legendre rules, written in radicals, are exact through degrees five and seven. Transported to [-1,1], the midpoint rule, the two-point rule, and these two rules are Gaussian rules for the unit weight, and the nodal polynomial of the n-point rule is the monic Legendre polynomial of degree n, defined as the monic orthogonal polynomial of that weight, for n=1,2,3,4. For n=2 and any a<b, every Gaussian rule for the unit weight on [a,b] has the transported two-point nodes and weights and the same value as the two-point QuadratureRule.

Proof for Theorem 10.101
uses 0

Exactness through degree 2n-1 is a finite list of moment identities, each checked by normal-form arithmetic using (\sqrt{3/5})^2=\tfrac35 or the squares of the four-point radicals. Positivity of the weights and the ordering of the nodes are inequalities between radicals. The characterization theorem then identifies each nodal polynomial with the monic Legendre polynomial, and for n=2 it pins down the nodes, whose weights are then fixed by exactness.

Beyond four points the nodes are no longer convenient radicals, and the library certifies them instead. A sparse rational polynomial p with \int_{-1}^1p\,x^k\,dx=0 for k<n, a condition checked in rational arithmetic from the moments of x^k, is the monic Legendre polynomial of degree n as soon as it is monic of degree n. Its roots are isolated by certified brackets (root brackets): a rational interval with a sign change at the ends and a derivative enclosure of fixed sign, so exactly one root lies inside. Ordered disjoint brackets inside (-1,1) then define a Gaussian rule at any order n, with no stored table of nodes.

used by 1✓L∃∀N

Let p be a sparse rational polynomial and let n valid root brackets for p be ordered, each strictly to the left of the next. The bracketed roots are strictly increasing and lie in their brackets. If p is monic of degree n over \mathbb R, its nodal polynomial on these roots is p itself. If moreover the brackets lie inside (-1,1) and the rational moments \int_{-1}^1p(x)x^k\,dx vanish for k<n, the roots are the nodes of a Gaussian rule for the unit weight on [-1,1], with the interpolatory weights.

Proof for Theorem 10.102
uses 0

Each valid bracket contains a unique root, and the ordering of the brackets orders the roots. A monic polynomial of degree n with n distinct roots is the product of the corresponding linear factors. The vanishing moments, extended linearly to every q of degree below n, make the nodal polynomial orthogonal to lower degrees; the Gaussian exactness and weight positivity arguments then apply without change.

The weights of a certified rule are enclosed from the same brackets. At a simple root r of p the Lagrange basis polynomial is p(x)/\bigl((x-r)\,p'(r)\bigr), so the Christoffel number is

w_r=\frac{1}{p'(r)}\int_{-1}^1\frac{p(x)}{x-r}\,dx.

Synthetic division writes the integral as a polynomial in r with rational coefficients, so the weight is a rational function of the single root r, and interval evaluation over the bracket encloses it.

Proof for Theorem 10.103
uses 0

The Lagrange basis polynomial at a node is the nodal polynomial divided by x-r_i and by the nodal weight, which equals p'(r_i) for a simple root. The division by x-r is carried out monomial by monomial through (x^k-r^k)/(x-r)=\sum_{j<k}x^jr^{k-1-j}, and integrating the result term by term gives \tilde p. The bracket's direction fixes the sign of p' on it, so dividing the numerator enclosure by the derivative enclosure is sound.

10.8.1.4. Convergence of positive rules🔗

The error formula needs 2n derivatives, and the constant M_{2n}/(2n)! need not stay small for a function that is merely continuous. A different argument gives convergence for every continuous f, and it uses exactly one property beyond exactness: positive weights.

Let w be continuous on [a,b] and let Q_n be rules with nonnegative weights and nodes in [a,b], where Q_n integrates every polynomial of degree at most d_n exactly against w and d_n\to\infty. Then Q_n(f)\to\int_a^b f\,w for every f continuous on [a,b]. This is the theorem of Pólya and Steklov. The same statement holds for normalized rules with nonnegative weights transported to [a,b].

Proof for Theorem 10.104
uses 0

Exactness on constants makes the weights of Q_n sum to \int_a^b w. If a polynomial p of degree at most d_n is within \delta of f on [a,b], positivity bounds |Q_n(f)-Q_n(p)| by \delta\int_a^b w, and |\int_a^b (p-f)w| is at most \delta\int_a^b|w|. Since Q_n(p) is the integral of p w, the error on f is at most \delta(\int_a^b w+\int_a^b|w|), a bound independent of n. The Weierstrass theorem supplies p for every \delta>0, and d_n\to\infty makes p admissible for all large n.

A Gauss rule with n+1 nodes is positive, has its nodes in [a,b], and has degree 2n+1, so the theorem applies directly.

Proof for Theorem 10.105
uses 0

The rules are positive with nodes in [a,b] and are exact to degree 2(n+1)-1, which tends to infinity. Apply the Pólya–Steklov theorem.

Positivity is not a technicality. The figure integrates the Runge function 1/(1+25x^2) over [-1,1] with the closed Newton–Cotes rule and the Gauss–Legendre rule, n=2,\dots,24 points. Both are exact to degree at least n-1, so both would converge if only exactness mattered. Newton–Cotes weights become negative at nine points and from eleven points on, the sum \sum_i|w_i| grows geometrically, and the error grows with it. The Gauss weights stay positive, their absolute sum is always 2, and the error decreases steadily. The divergence of Newton–Cotes is a classical computation shown here for contrast; the library proves the positive side.

10.8.1.5. Panel rules of any order🔗

For a smooth integrand the practical way to reduce error is to cut the interval into N equal panels and apply a low-order rule on each. The only information the composite construction needs about the local rule is a one-panel bound of the form

\left\|\int_a^b f-Q(f)\right\|\le\frac{M\,(b-a)^{m+1}}{D} \qquad\text{whenever }\|f^{(m)}\|\le M\text{ on }[a,b].

Summing N such bounds over panels of length (b-a)/N gives C(b-a)^{m+1}/(DN^m). The library records the pair (rule, D) with the proof of the one-panel bound as a PanelRule m, and builds composite certificates, tolerance planning, and adaptive bisection once for every order m.

A panel rule of order m is a normalized rule Q with a positive constant D and a proof that, on every ordered interval [a,b], every f\in C^m[a,b] with \|f^{(m)}\|\le M there satisfies \|\int_a^b f-Q(f)\|\le M(b-a)^{m+1}/D. Its composite certificate on N>0 equal panels, given a panelwise derivative bounder with common bound C, has error budget C(b-a)^{m+1}/(DN^m). Simpson's rule and the two-point Gauss–Legendre rule are panel rules of order four.

On an ordered interval, for f\in C^2[a,b] with \|f''\|\le C there,

\left\|\int_a^bf-\frac{b-a}2\bigl(f(a)+f(b)\bigr)\right\| \le\frac{C(b-a)^3}{12},\qquad \left\|\int_a^bf-(b-a)f\!\left(\tfrac{a+b}2\right)\right\| \le\frac{C(b-a)^3}{24}.

Both rules are exact through degree one, and they are panel rules of order two with D=12 and D=24.

Proof for Theorem 10.107
uses 0

Two integrations by parts write each error as \int_a^bK(t)f''(t)\,dt. For the trapezoid rule the kernel is (t-a)(b-t)/2\ge0, of mass (b-a)^3/12. For the midpoint rule it is (t-a)^2/2 on the left half and (b-t)^2/2 on the right, of mass (b-a)^3/24. Bound f'' by C.

The figure measures the composite error for \int_0^1e^x\,dx against the panel count on logarithmic axes. On the left are the two second-order rules, on the right Simpson's rule and the two-point Gauss rule. Each measured error sits below its dashed proved bound e/(DN^m), and each curve has slope -m, so halving the panel width divides the error by 4 or by 16. The constants fall in the order the denominators 12, 24, 2880, 4320 predict: at every panel count the midpoint error is about half the trapezoid error, and the Gauss error about two thirds of Simpson's.

Because the budget is an explicit function of N, the number of panels needed for a tolerance \varepsilon can be computed in advance. The planner never evaluates the integrand; it needs only the derivative bound C.

uses 1used by 0✓L∃∀N

Let m\ne0, D>0, a\le b, C\ge0 and \varepsilon>0, put B=C(b-a)^{m+1}/D, and let N=\max(1,\lceil(B/\varepsilon)^{1/m}\rceil). Then B/N^m\le\varepsilon. Consequently, for a panel rule of order m, an integrand in C^m[a,b], a<b, and a derivative bounder whose bound on every subinterval is at most C, the composite certificate on the planned mesh has error budget at most \varepsilon, and its value is within \varepsilon of \int_a^bf.

Proof for Theorem 10.108
uses 0

The ceiling gives N\ge(B/\varepsilon)^{1/m}, and raising both sides to the power m gives N^m\ge B/\varepsilon. The composite budget is B/N^m, and certificate soundness bounds the actual error by the budget.

For m=4 we use the classical one-panel constants for Simpson's rule and the two-point Gauss rule. We prove their composite bounds and choose meshes with planners in exact rational arithmetic that run inside Lean.

Proof for Theorem 10.109
uses 0

Represent the Simpson error as the integral of the fourth derivative against its Peano kernel, whose two polynomial pieces live on [a,(a+b)/2] and [(a+b)/2,b]; four integrations by parts produce it, and cubic exactness cancels all boundary polynomial terms. The kernel has fixed sign and exact mass (b-a)^5/2880. Bounding the fourth derivative by C gives the stated norm estimate.

The composite rule has a canonical flattened list of ordered weighted terms. Its exact-real weighted sum is proved equal to the analytic composite Simpson value. Verified rational, interval, or floating-point evaluators can therefore evaluate the same term list.

For the canonical panel-major list T_N(f,a,b),

\operatorname{weightedSum}\!\left(T_N(f,a,b)\right) =S_N(f;[a,b]).

The canonical term list fixes the nodes and accumulation order; this equality certifies its exact-real value. Equality of sums alone would not fix an order.

uses 0

If B<0 the bound holds for every N. Otherwise the ceiling construction gives N\geq(B/\tau)^{1/4} and N\geq1. Positivity permits raising the first inequality to the fourth power, yielding N^4\geq B/\tau. Rearranging with \tau>0 proves B/N^4\leq\tau.

Given root-interval smoothness and certified panelwise fourth-derivative bounds, the planned Simpson and two-point Gauss–Legendre constructors return ordinary QuadratureCerts whose semantic error is at most the user's positive tolerance. The public conclusion refers only to the integral, computed rule value, and tolerance; panel selection remains an internal construction.

For either planned fourth-order rule Q_{N(\tau)},

\left|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx-Q_{N(\tau)}(f)\right| \leq\tau.

Mathlib's composite trapezoidal rule is exposed through the common certificate interface. Assume f is C^2 on S=[\min(a,b),\max(a,b)] and |D^2_S f(x)|\leq\zeta for every real x, where D^2_S denotes the second iterated within-derivative. For N>0 subintervals the error is at most |b-a|^3\zeta/(12N^2).

Under these same regularity and derivative-bound hypotheses, for a positive tolerance the checked planner chooses N=\max(1,\lceil\sqrt{B/\mathrm{tolerance}}\rceil) with B=|b-a|^3\zeta/12. The bound forces \zeta\ge 0, and the resulting composite trapezoidal certificate has error at most the requested tolerance. The square-root choice retains the standard O(\mathrm{tolerance}^{-1/2}) mesh scaling.

A QuadratureTree records a rule-independent binary subdivision. Each leaf contains an ordinary local quadrature certificate and integrability evidence; adjacent children compose by interval-integral additivity. The root therefore certifies the sum of all leaf values with the sum of their error budgets. An adaptive tactic or external checker may choose the tree; soundness does not depend on that choice.

If \mathcal L(T) is the set of leaves, then the root certificate states

\left\|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx -\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal L(T)}Q_\ell\right\| \leq\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal L(T)}E_\ell.

Proof for Theorem 10.123
uses 0

Induct on the binary tree. A leaf is exactly its stored local certificate. At a branch, interval-integral additivity splits the root integral across the two adjacent children; apply the two inductive estimates and the triangle inequality. Their values and budgets add, giving the recursively stored root certificate.
